title: Should the US publicly subsidize unique/original films like other countries do?

commenti.body:
1. We already do. Most states have film production grants. I’m originally from North Dakota, and just a few years ago, they provided a significant portion of the budget for what is the largest indie production done in-state. Up until then, ND was one of the few states that didn’t have a program for this.

2. What evidence do you have that film is dying as an art form? More independent productions get made every year now than in any decade since the 1920s. The resources to make and then distribute media have never been more accessible. The downside to everyone being able to create is that now it’s much harder to get noticed and there’s a critical lack of quality control. If anything, we need more gatekeeping.

3. I don’t think there’s any need for nationalizing or otherwise vastly expanding a film production grant program. The United States’ most significant contributions to cinema have been in the form of Hollywood’s unmatched scale and commercial appeal, and that machine has more or less worked fine for a hundred years. It goes through rough patches, like the one it’s in right now, but they’ll get it figured out eventually.

I think it’s a great idea and have a feeling we’ll have something like this someday. It’s what happens before that that concerns me. 

I think of my home state, Alaska, which had a pretty successful tax incentive program to film movies here and the legislature blew it up. Not least of which was because red-area legislators didn’t want to subsidize “Hollywood.” Of course thats not the same idea but I say it because voters were fine with blowing up a desperately needed new industry in its infancy to spite their own faces. That was a few years ago and now we’re even more entrenched in the culture war. I think we’ll have to get through this first and see a shift in Americans’ attitudes toward how public funds are used.

As mentioned, plenty of states have film production grants or offer tax breaks for film and TV production. Tons of films and TV shows are shot in Georgia because Georgia offers some of the most substantial tax breaks of any state in the country.

Two, the US government *does* subsidize and support films. It's just that they support films that positively portray the US military. Every single Marvel film is backed by the Pentagon and many, many other high budget action films are the same way. Basically any film you see with actual US military equipment (which includes anything from uniforms to actual military hardware) has likely been supported by the US government.

Whether that's a good thing is subjective (fwiw I think it's bad that Hollywood tacitly creates military propaganda and that the government has set up an environment where nearly any military film being made in the US needs their approval) but it's not correct to say that the government doesn't support the film industry. They do it differently than the countries you mentioned, though.

Also I don't buy the idea that film is dying in the first place. The US studio system is enduring one of its most troubled periods in decades, yes, but the studio system isn't the end all be all of the film industry as a whole. People have been writing about the death of film practically since its birth as a medium.

1) I am not talking about the tax breaks and economic incentives that currently exist for film productions. Those primarily exist to generate economic activity in the area and go to any movie that shoots in the area. They do not exist to subsidize films based on their originality/artistic merit/etc. which is what I'm proposing.

2) It's a qualitative judgement and so it's difficult to prove empirically. But any number of film makers from Martin Scorsese to David Lynch to Charlie Kaufman will tell you that the business takes far fewer risks than it used to. Someone like David Lynch used to regularly get budgets in the tens of millions of dollars for his films, now he has trouble getting anything funded. A movie as weird as Mulholland Drive could get a budget that was the modern day equivalent of 25 million dollars, and it actually turned a profit! That would never happen today. A24 seemed to be the one saving grace, [but they've said they're going to shift away from auteur cinema](https://www.thefader.com/2023/10/11/report-a24-to-expand-produce-more-commercial-films) and move towards more commercial fair because their current path isn't financially sustainable.  


Admittedly the issue is partially the audience. People aren't as willing to dedicate their time and energy to challenging films as they use to. In 1999, a 29 year old kid could get the modern day equivalent of 70 million dollars to make a 190 minute original drama film (Magnolia), and it could actually make a decent profit. That would never happen today in a million years. But even if there isn't as much demand for challenging and original films, there is still value in their creation, so they should be subsidized. Just like we subsidize art museums and libraries even though there's not enough demand for them to exist without those subsidies. There's inherent value in their existence.  


Honestly the only film that has blown me away in years is Aftersun, and it's no surprise that that movie got a lot of its funding from the Scottish film fund. It's challenging and fairly non-narrative, so I don't think it would've gotten funded otherwise.

It’s a bigger problem than just finding a way to fund movies outside of the Hollywood system.

Say you can finance a film. Are you going to be able to pay yourself something that you can live off of? How about your cast and crew? Probably not, so now all of those people are going to have to have other jobs to provide a living for themselves. That means they’re going to have less time and energy to devote to the work, which means it won’t be as good. This is the biggest barrier I’ve found in trying to be an independent filmmaker. 

You need to build a middle class for film artists to foster creative, independent work. The problem is that the industry is monopolized by one small group of people. If there were more regional film industries, money would be more diffused and there would be more jobs related to these industries that people could use to support themselves. 

That’s just not gonna happen anytime soon though.

Between Wokeness, fascism, and AI, The US no longer has anything of value to say. Just let Scorcese and Tarantino play out their careers and let the rest of it die. Leave the industry to real (human) artists.

Eventually every movie would end up Top Gun-ish. We're a very militaristic society. The government would sell a movie to the military in a heartbeat. Guarantee they would find a loophole, at least.

Words Words Words
